title: Unraveling the Controls of Soil Moisture and Atmospheric Water Demand on Critical Soil Moisture Variability Across Indian Biomes
content:
Abstract

The critical soil moisture (CSM) threshold marks the transition from energy-to water-limited vegetation functioning, constraining photosynthesis and evapotranspiration. Although often treated as a fixed ecosystem property, its sensitivity to vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and soil moisture (SM) during drydowns remains poorly understood. Shifting from high-to low-VPD drydowns across India redistributes land-atmosphere coupling: ∼24.8% of grids shift from transitional (Regime 2) to transitional-to-wet (Regime 4), especially in the northwest, west-central, northeast, and Western Ghats. In contrast, low-SM drydowns shift ∼35.2% toward transitional regimes across the Indo-Gangetic Plains, Deccan Plateau, and central-eastern India, showing that high VPD and low SM independently affect water limitation. Biome-specific analyses demonstrate that CSM is a dynamic rather than a stationary property of the plant-soil continuum. High VPD produces the largest CSM reductions in deciduous forests mosaic pixels (−11.23 ± 0.36 kg m−2), whereas low SM has the strongest effect in savannas mosaic pixels (−14.05 ± 0.31 kg m−2). By explicitly separating SM and VPD coupling, we show that SM dominates CSM variability, with VPD mainly acting through its interaction with SM, as evident in croplands and grasslands. In terms of days spent in a water-limited regime, ecosystems such as croplands, grasslands, and savanna mosaics are particularly vulnerable to compound high-VPD and low-SM conditions, whereas evergreen forests are comparatively resilient to atmospheric demand but highly sensitive to SM depletion. Together, these findings demonstrate the non-stationary nature of CSM and biome-specific vulnerabilities to intensifying hydroclimatic extremes under climate change.
